fact: The Moon's surface gravity is about 1.62 m/s², roughly one-sixth of Earth's 9.81 m/s².
Mars pulls at about 3.71 m/s², around 38% of Earth's gravity.
Jupiter's gravity at its cloud tops is about 24.8 m/s², roughly 2.5 times Earth's.
In 1971, Apollo 15's David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon. With no air, they hit the ground together.
Newton published his law of universal gravitation in the Principia in 1687.
To escape Earth's gravity without further thrust, you'd need about 11.2 km per second.
Astronauts on the ISS float because they're in constant free fall. Gravity up there is still about 90% of what it is on the ground.
Einstein's general relativity (1915) describes gravity as the curving of space and time by mass.
LIGO first detected gravitational waves on September 14, 2015, from two black holes merging over a billion light-years away.
Ocean tides come mostly from the Moon's gravity. The Sun's tidal effect is a little under half as strong.
A neutron star's surface gravity is on the order of a hundred billion times Earth's.
Pluto's surface gravity is about 0.62 m/s², around 6% of Earth's.
A belly-down skydiver reaches a terminal speed of roughly 200 km/h (about 120 mph).
GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day relative to the ground, mainly because gravity is weaker up there. The system corrects for it.
Gravity is a little weaker at the equator (about 9.78 m/s²) than at the poles (about 9.83 m/s²).
The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.
Changes in gravity travel at the speed of light. If the Sun vanished, Earth would keep orbiting for about 8 minutes.
The Moon drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year. Laser reflectors left by Apollo measure it.
Tidal friction is slowly lengthening Earth's day, by roughly 2 milliseconds per century.
In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in galaxy M87.
Gravity is by far the weakest of the four fundamental forces. Between two protons it's about 10³⁶ times weaker than electromagnetism.
NASA reports that astronauts can lose around 1–1.5% of bone mass per month in microgravity without countermeasures.
Venus's surface gravity is about 8.87 m/s², around 90% of Earth's.
Saturn is huge but not dense, so gravity at its cloud tops (about 10.4 m/s²) is close to Earth's.
The James Webb Space Telescope orbits near L2, a gravitational balance point about 1.5 million km from Earth.
Voyager 2 used gravity assists from Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. It's still the only spacecraft to visit the last two.
In 1798 Henry Cavendish measured the tiny gravitational pull between lead spheres, which effectively 'weighed' the Earth.
A scale that reads 70 kg on Earth would read about 11.6 kg on the Moon.
Fighter pilots with g-suits can tolerate around 9 g, nine times their body weight, for short periods.
The falling-apple story comes from Newton himself, recounted by his friend William Stukeley. No, it didn't hit his head.
Black holes don't 'suck'. From far away, a black hole pulls just like any other object with the same mass.
